catalog_quote: The following list comprises all the elementary sounds that occur in the Australian dialects, so far as our observation has extended. ... The general character of the pronunciation is dental and nasal; the sounds are formed principally in the fore part of the mouth, and the intonations are varied and pleasing. The accent, in words of two syllables, is usually on the first, and in words of three or more on the antepenultimate; but to this there are many exceptions. Words and syllables always end in a vowel, or in one of the consonants, l, m, n, ŋ, and r.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (Hale 1846, archive.org scanned). The quoted passage is at the stated locator: running head 'AUSTRALIA. 483', 'PHONOLOGY.' heading at scanned line ~40497, accent sentence at lines 40547-40550: 'The accent, in words of two syllables, is usually on the first, and in words of three or more on the antepenultimate; but to this there are many exceptions. Words and syllables always end in a vowel, or in one of the consonants, /, m, n, y, and r.' The only differences from the report's quote are scanned glyph renderings (l -> '/', engma -> 'y') and the marked ellipsis; the opening sentence 'The following list comprises all the elementary sounds that occur in the Australian dialects, so far as…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent on the first syllable of disyllables and on the antepenultimate syllable of words of three or more syllables (i.e. also the first syllable in trisyllables; third-from-last in longer, typically suffixed, words), with 'many exceptions'. Impressionistic 19th-century observation.
new_statements.exceptions: 'but to this there are many exceptions' (none itemised for Wiradurei; in the Kamilarai [Awabakal] column Hale notes accent shift in certain declensional forms, e.g. mákoro -> makáro).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent in citation forms. IMPORTANT: the sentence is Hale's generalisation over 'the Australian dialects, so far as our observation has extended', i.e. chiefly Threlkeld's Lake Macquarie/Hunter River language (his 'Kamilarai' = Awabakal) and the Wellington Valley Wiradurei he studied with Rev. W. Watson (c. 200 words taken down by Hale himself); it is not stated separately for Wiradurei. Modern NSW-wide guides seen only in snippet/secondary form (Thieberger & McGregor 1994 general guide; Reid 2010) instead describe first-syllable main stress, with long vowels attracting stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Hale's 'Wira-durei / Wiraiurai' is the Wellington Valley (Macquarie River) variety of Wiradhuri = wira1262, described from Rev. William Watson's mission materials plus Hale's own elicitation (1839-40). However the accent sentence is worded as a generalisation over 'the Australian dialects' Hale observed, i.e. jointly for his 'Kamilarai' (= Threlkeld's Hunter River-Lake Macquarie language, Awabakal, awab1243) and Wiradurei; it is not a Wiradhuri-only statement. Günther/Fraser 1892 ('Wirradhuri/Wiradhari', Wellington) and Mathews 1904 ('Wiradyuri') are the same language and are silent on accent.
